q: Her prayers, however, moved the Gods, {and} moved their parents. For the color of the fruit, when it has fully ripened, is black;[26] and what was left of them, from the funeral pile, reposed in the same urn.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: the Gods are moved by Her prayers (and moved their parents)
q: Her prayers, however, moved the Gods, {and} moved their parents. For the color of the fruit, when it has fully ripened, is black;[26] and what was left of them, from the funeral pile, reposed in the same urn.”

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: three daughters of Minyas work at textile tasks (during the festival)
q: The daughters of Minyas alone, within doors, interrupting the festival with unseasonable labor,[14] are either carding wool, or twirling the threads with their fingers, or are plying at the web, and keeping the handmaids to their work.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Minyas has daughters three daughters of Minyas
q: But Alcithoë, the daughter of Minyas,[1] does not think that the rites[2] of the God ought to be received; but still, in her rashness, denies that Bacchus is the progeny of Jupiter; and she has her sisters[3] as partners in her impiety.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus is a God
q: The priest had ordered both mistresses and maids, laying aside their employments, to have their breasts covered with skins, and to loosen the fillets of their hair, and {to put} garlands on their locks, and to take the verdant thyrsi in their hands; and had prophesied that severe would be the resentment of the Deity, {if} affronted.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has attribute everlasting youth
q: For thine is youth everlasting; thou art a boy to all time, thou art beheld {as} the most beauteous {of all} in high heaven; thou hast the features of a virgin, when thou standest without thy horns.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus conquers East (as far as India and the Ganges)
q: By thee the East was conquered, as far as where swarthy India is bounded by the remote Ganges.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus is followed by Bacchanals
q: The Bacchanals and the Satyrs follow {thee}; the drunken old man, too, {Silenus}, who supports his reeling limbs with a staff, and sticks by no means very fast to his bending ass.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Alcithoë is a daughter (of Minyas)
q: Alcithoë was the daughter of Minyas, who, according to some, was the son of Orchomenus, according to others, his father.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus festivals is a religious rites (celebrated by Bacchus’s worshippers)
q: Thus, the daughters of Minyas are said to have been changed into bats, solely because they neglected to join in the orgies of that God;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Bromius (from the cries and noise of his worshippers)
q: Bacchus was called Bromius, from βρέμω, ‘to cry out,’ or ‘shout,’ from the yells and noise made by his worshippers, whose peculiar cries were, Εὐοῖ Βάκχε, ὦ Ἰακχε, Ιώ Βάκχε, Εὐοῖ σαβοῖ.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Lyæus (because wine dispels care)
q: Bacchus was called Lyæus, from the Greek word, λύειν, ‘to loosen,’ or ‘relax,’ because wine dispels care.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Thyoneus (from Semele, or from frenzy)
q: Bacchus was called Thyoneus, either from Semele, his mother, one of whose names was Thyone, or from the Greek, θύειν, ‘to be frantic,’ from which origin the Bacchanals also received their name of Thyades.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Lenæus (from the wine-press)
q: From the Greek word λῆνος, ‘a wine-press.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Nyctelius (because his orgies were celebrated by night)
q: From the Greek word νὺξ, ‘night,’ because his orgies were celebrated by night.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Eleleus (from the Greek shout ελελεῦ)
q: Eleleus is from the shout, or ‘huzza’ of the Greeks, which was ελελεῦ.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Iacchus (from clamor or noise)
q: From the Greek ἰαχὴ, ‘clamor,’ or ‘noise.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has name Evan (from the Bacchanals’ exclamation Εὐοῖ)
q: From the exclamation, Εὐοῖ, or ‘Evoë’ which the Bacchanals used in performing his orgies.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has mother Semele (his mortal mother)
q: Bacchus was called Thyoneus, either from Semele, his mother, one of whose names was Thyone,

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Alcithoë has sister Aristippe
q: The names of the sisters of Alcithoë, according to Plutarch, were Aristippe and Leucippe.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus has parent Jupiter (Jupiter undertook the duties of a mother during his gestation)
q: The word ‘bimater’ seems to have been fancied by Ovid as an appropriate epithet for Bacchus, Jupiter having undertaken the duties of a mother for him, in the latter months of gestation.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: three daughters of Minyas is a women (who opposed joining the orgies of Bacchus)
q: Thus, the daughters of Minyas are said to have been changed into bats, solely because they neglected to join in the orgies of that God;
